stem: A retail pharmacist has a collaborative practice agreement with a physician. A 16-year-old who has never been referred by that physician asks the pharmacist to manage a chronic disease under the agreement. Which issue is most important?

choices.text: Retail CDTM applies to every patient who enters the pharmacy if the pharmacist is licensed.
The pharmacist may proceed if the medication is inexpensive.
The patient’s age is irrelevant because CDTM has no patient-scope limits.
The pharmacist may replace referral with a technician’s approval.
Retail CDTM is limited by statutory patient, referral, consent, disease, agreement, and setting restrictions; the stated facts do not automatically fit that scope.

explanation.core_reasoning: A retail CDTM agreement does not create universal disease-management authority. The pharmacist must first confirm that the patient and proposed activity fit the referred, consenting-adult and agreement-specific statutory scope.

choice_analysis.A: Licensure alone does not remove the retail CDTM scope restrictions.
choice_analysis.B: Medication price has no role in establishing CDTM patient eligibility.
choice_analysis.C: The retail statutory pathway includes patient-scope restrictions, so age can be material.
choice_analysis.D: A technician cannot substitute for the statutory referral and consent framework.
choice_analysis.E: This recognizes that retail CDTM authority depends on multiple scope predicates, several of which are absent here.

related_facts: CDTM scope is defined by the authorizing law and the written collaborative agreement.
Referral and consent are legal predicates, not optional workflow preferences.
explanation.mpje_trap: Do not treat the existence of a CDTM agreement as permission to manage any patient for any condition.

reasoning_steps: Identify that the setting is retail CDTM
Check the patient/referral/consent predicates before considering drug therapy
